track.name: Frontend testing
track.blurb: Interview questions on frontend testing: strategy, unit and component tests, mocking with MSW, Playwright E2E, visual and performance testing, CI and flaky tests.

questions.q: What is the testing pyramid, and how does the testing trophy differ from it?
questions.answer:
**The testing pyramid says write many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and very few end-to-end tests. The testing trophy, from Kent C. Dodds, keeps few E2E tests but adds static analysis as a base layer and puts most effort into integration tests, because for UI code those give the most confidence per unit of cost.**

**The pyramid** (Mike Cohn, popularised by Martin Fowler) came from a time when E2E tests were slow and flaky and unit tests ran in milliseconds. The shape optimises for speed and precise failures:

```text
      /\        E2E: few
     /--\       Integration: some
    /----\      Unit: many
```

**The trophy** reshapes it for frontends:

```text
     [ E2E ]          a handful of critical journeys
   ( Integration )    most tests: feature rendered with real children,
                      real state, network mocked
     [ Unit ]         pure logic only
   [  Static  ]       TypeScript + ESLint, always on
```

Why the change makes sense for UI:
- A "unit" test of a component with every child mocked mostly checks that you wrote the JSX you wrote. Bugs live in the wiring: props, state transitions, effects, conditional rendering.
- Modern tools (React Testing Library, MSW) make integration tests fast enough, typically tens to hundreds of milliseconds each.
- Integration tests that query by role and text survive refactors, so maintenance cost is lower than for implementation-coupled unit tests.
- Static types remove a whole class of bugs (wrong prop, typo, null access) without any test code.

**Where they agree**: E2E tests are expensive and should cover only the journeys that matter most, such as sign-in, checkout and publishing.

**Neither is a law.** The right shape depends on where your bugs come from. A date or pricing library should be unit-test heavy. A CRUD dashboard is integration heavy. Spotify's "testing honeycomb" argues the same for microservices: test services through their real boundaries.

A practical rule that reconciles both: push each assertion down to the cheapest layer that can still catch the bug.
followUps: Which shape fits a pricing library versus a CRUD dashboard?
Why did E2E tests end up at the top of both shapes?
Where does TypeScript fit in a testing strategy?
mistakes: Reciting a shape as a law without explaining the cost and confidence reasoning behind it.
Forgetting static analysis as a layer.
Treating a fully mocked component test as a meaningful unit test.

questions.q: How do you decide what to test and what not to test in a frontend codebase?
questions.answer:
**I test behaviour a user or another developer depends on: what renders in each state, what happens on interaction, business rules, contracts at boundaries, and every bug we fix. I skip implementation details, trivial markup and third-party library behaviour. The question I ask is: if this test fails, would a user see a bug?**

**Worth testing:**
- **User-visible behaviour per state**: loading, empty, error, success, permission denied. Many production bugs are an unhandled state.
- **Business rules**: pricing, discounts, permissions, validation, date boundaries and timezones. These cost money when wrong.
- **Interactions**: submit, keyboard navigation, undo, optimistic updates and their rollback.
- **Contracts**: API response shapes you depend on (typed mocks or contract tests) and the public props of shared components other teams use.
- **Regressions**: every bug fix comes with a test that fails before and passes after.
- **Accessibility basics**: role-based queries plus automated axe checks on key screens.

**Usually not worth testing:**
- Internal state values, private helpers, CSS class names. Kent C. Dodds' "Testing Implementation Details" frames these as tests that break on safe refactors (false negatives) and pass when behaviour is broken (false positives).
- Framework or library behaviour (that React re-renders, that the router matches a path).
- Static markup with no logic.
- Large snapshot dumps of component trees.

**Choosing the layer** is part of the decision:

| What | Layer |
| --- | --- |
| "Codes are case-insensitive" | unit test of the pricing function |
| "Applying a code updates the total" | integration test with RTL and MSW |
| "A user can pay and gets a confirmation" | one E2E test |

**Prioritise by risk**: frequency of change times cost of failure. A checkout page that changes weekly deserves more tests than a static about page. Also look at your bug history: if most incidents come from API contract changes, invest in contract tests, not more unit tests.

**Trade-off to name**: every test is maintenance. Deleting a test that breaks often and has never caught a bug is a valid improvement.
followUps: Would you test a purely presentational component?
How does bug history change your priorities?
When is deleting a test the right call?
mistakes: Answering only 'everything' or quoting a coverage number.
Testing internal state or class names instead of user-visible behaviour.
Not mentioning regression tests for fixed bugs.

questions.q: How would you introduce a testing strategy to a large frontend codebase that has almost no tests?
questions.answer:
**I would not try to backfill coverage. I would switch on the free safety nets first (strict types, lint), add a small smoke E2E suite for the money paths so catastrophic breakage is caught immediately, then grow integration tests where code changes, with a rule that every bug fix and every touched feature gets a test. And I would make the suite fast and reliable from day one, because a slow flaky suite gets ignored.**

**Step by step:**

1. **Free layer (week 1)**: TypeScript `strict` (incrementally, per directory if needed), ESLint with `react-hooks`, `testing-library` and `jest-dom` plugins. This catches real bugs with no test code.
2. **Smoke E2E (weeks 1-2)**: 3 to 5 Playwright tests for the journeys that make money or would be catastrophic to break: sign-in, the core create flow, checkout. Run them against a production build in CI on every PR.
3. **Test infrastructure**: Vitest, RTL, MSW with shared handlers, data factories and a `renderWithProviders` helper. The cost of writing the first test in a feature must be minutes, not hours.
4. **Grow where change happens**: a rule in the PR template and review: changes to a feature include an integration test for the behaviour touched; bug fixes include a regression test. Coverage then grows where risk is, not where it is easy.
5. **Extract logic**: as features are touched, pull business rules out of components into pure functions and unit test them.
6. **Make it visible**: track suite duration, flake rate and escaped bugs, not just coverage.

```text
risk-based order
  high change + high cost (checkout, auth)    -> first
  high change + low cost (internal admin)     -> as touched
  low change + high cost (billing exports)    -> targeted tests
  low change + low cost (marketing pages)     -> smoke only
```

**Getting buy-in** matters as much as tooling: pair with engineers on the first tests, show a bug the smoke suite caught, and keep CI time low so testing feels like help.

**Mistakes I would avoid**: a coverage target imposed globally (it produces assertion-free tests), a giant E2E suite as the main strategy (slow, flaky, expensive to debug), and big-bang "testing sprints" that stop feature work and produce low-value tests.

**Why this order works**: the smoke suite gives protection on day one, and the "test what you touch" rule concentrates new tests in the most-changed modules, which is where most bugs are introduced, without a dedicated testing project that stops feature work.
followUps: How do you get buy-in from a team that sees tests as slowing them down?
What would you measure to show progress?
Which tests would you write in the first week?
mistakes: Proposing a big-bang backfill or a global coverage target.
Starting with a large E2E suite as the main safety net.
Ignoring suite speed and flakiness, which decide whether the team keeps using tests.

questions.q: Why is 100% code coverage a poor goal, and what would you measure instead?
questions.answer:
**Coverage tells you which code never ran during tests, not whether anything was verified. Chasing 100% produces assertion-free tests of trivial code and makes the suite expensive to change, while still missing bugs. I use coverage as a map of gaps, and measure what actually matters: escaped bugs, branch coverage on critical modules, mutation score on core logic, and suite speed and flakiness.**

**Why the number misleads:**
- A test that renders a component and asserts nothing yields high coverage and zero confidence.
- Line coverage hides branches: `return a && b ? x : y` is one line with several paths.
- Files no test imports may not appear in the report at all unless the coverage config includes them, which inflates the percentage.
- Global thresholds get gamed under deadline pressure.
- The last 10 to 20% is usually defensive error handling and glue code where tests are costly and low value.

**What I would measure instead:**

| Signal | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Branch coverage on critical paths (pricing, auth, permissions) | where bugs are expensive |
| Coverage on changed lines in a PR | stops new untested code without gaming old code |
| Mutation score on core logic (e.g. Stryker) | answers "would tests notice if this code were wrong?" |
| Escaped defects: bugs found in production that tests should have caught | the outcome you care about |
| Suite duration and flake rate | a slow or flaky suite gets ignored |

**Mutation testing** in one line: the tool mutates code (flips `>` to `>=`, deletes a call) and reruns tests; a surviving mutant shows behaviour no test checks. It is slow, so I apply it to small, important modules.

**Practical config** in Vitest:

```ts
coverage: {
  provider: "v8",
  include: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"],
  thresholds: { "src/billing/**": { branches: 90 } },
}
```

**When a number is useful**: as a ratchet that must not go down, or as a threshold on specific critical directories. When a team has almost no tests, rising coverage is a fine progress indicator, as long as reviewers check that the tests assert meaningful behaviour.
followUps: What is mutation testing and when is it worth the cost?
Would you enforce a coverage threshold in CI?
How can coverage reports be misleading about unimported files?
mistakes: Equating executed code with verified behaviour.
Looking only at line coverage and missing branches.
Proposing a different arbitrary global percentage as the answer.

questions.q: Why would you choose Vitest over Jest for a new project, and what changes when you migrate?
questions.answer:
**For a new Vite-based or modern TypeScript project I would pick Vitest: it reuses the Vite config and transform pipeline, so TypeScript, JSX, ESM and path aliases work without a separate Babel or ts-jest setup, it has a fast watch mode, and its API is close enough to Jest that the migration is mostly mechanical. Jest is still a reasonable choice for existing large suites or React Native, where it remains the default.**

**Why Vitest:**
- **One pipeline**: the same plugins and aliases as your app; no duplicate transform config to drift.
- **ESM-native**: Jest's ESM support has historically needed experimental flags; Vitest treats ESM as the default.
- **Speed in watch mode**: reruns tests related to changed modules using Vite's module graph.
- **Built-in features**: TypeScript out of the box, v8 or istanbul coverage, in-source tests, a UI (`vitest --ui`), and browser mode for running tests in a real browser.
- **Jest-compatible API**: `describe`, `test`, `expect`, snapshot matchers, and `vi` in place of `jest`.

**What changes when migrating (from the Vitest migration guide and experience):**
- `jest.fn`, `jest.mock`, `jest.spyOn` become `vi.fn`, `vi.mock`, `vi.spyOn`.
- Globals are off by default: import from `vitest` or set `test.globals: true` (and add the types).
- `vi.mock` is hoisted like `jest.mock`, but a factory that wants a variable must use `vi.hoisted`; module mocks that returned a default export may need an explicit `default` key.
- `jest.requireActual` becomes `await vi.importActual()`.
- Test environment: set `environment: "jsdom"` (or `happy-dom`) explicitly.
- jest-dom: import `@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest` in the setup file.
- Some Jest-specific config (`moduleNameMapper`, `transform`) disappears because Vite handles it.
- Snapshot files may need regenerating if the serialised format differs slightly.

**Migration approach**: run both runners side by side for a short time, migrate directory by directory, and compare test counts so nothing silently stops running.

**When to stay on Jest**: a huge, stable suite with custom transformers and no Vite in the stack, or React Native projects. The gain has to be worth the churn.
followUps: How does vi.mock hoisting affect factories?
When would you keep Jest?
How would you verify nothing was lost during migration?
mistakes: Claiming Vitest is faster in every case without explaining why (shared Vite pipeline, ESM, watch mode).
Not knowing the practical migration steps such as globals, vi.importActual and jest-dom setup.

questions.q: What is snapshot testing with toMatchSnapshot, and why do many teams avoid it?
questions.answer:
**A snapshot test serialises some output (often a rendered component tree) to a file the first time it runs, then fails whenever the output differs. Many teams avoid large component snapshots because they fail on every harmless markup change, reviewers update them without reading, and they assert nothing specific about behaviour, so they create noise rather than confidence.**

**How it works:**

```tsx
test("renders the price tag", () => {
  const { container } = render(<PriceTag amount={4999} currency="INR" />);
  expect(container.firstChild).toMatchSnapshot(); // writes __snapshots__/price-tag.test.tsx.snap
});
```

Running with `-u` (or pressing `u` in watch mode) rewrites the stored snapshot.

**Why big snapshots go wrong:**
- **They encode everything**: class names, wrapper divs, attribute order. Any refactor changes them.
- **Rubber-stamping**: a 400-line diff in a `.snap` file gets accepted with `-u` because nobody can review it. At that point the test checks nothing.
- **No intent**: the snapshot does not say *what* matters. A reader cannot tell whether the currency symbol or the wrapper div is the important part.
- **False confidence**: coverage goes up, but bugs that render the wrong content on first run are frozen into the baseline.

**Where snapshots are fine:**
- Small, stable, meaningful outputs: a serialiser, a generated SQL string, an error message format, a CLI output.
- **Inline snapshots** (`toMatchInlineSnapshot()`) keep the expected value in the test file, short and reviewable.
- Data transformations where the output shape is the contract.

```ts
expect(formatPrice(4999, "INR")).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`"₹49.99"`);
```

**Better alternatives for components**: explicit assertions on what the user sees (`expect(screen.getByText("₹49.99")).toBeVisible()`), and for appearance, visual regression screenshots, which a human can actually review.

**A team rule that works**: no snapshot longer than about 20 lines, prefer inline snapshots, and a snapshot update in a PR must be explained in the description.
followUps: When are inline snapshots a good fit?
How is a visual screenshot test different from a DOM snapshot?
mistakes: Defending large component snapshots as a cheap way to raise coverage.
Not mentioning that reviewers rubber-stamp snapshot updates.

questions.q: Why does React Testing Library recommend querying by role, and what is the query priority?
questions.answer:
**Querying by role finds elements the way assistive technology and users do, by what they are (a button, a textbox, a heading) and their accessible name, so tests survive markup refactors and fail when the UI is inaccessible. The priority is: role, label text, placeholder, text, display value, then alt text and title, and test IDs only as a last resort.**

**The principle**: Testing Library's guiding principle is that the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give. Users do not see class names or component names; they see a "Save" button.

**The priority list from the Testing Library docs:**
1. Accessible to everyone: `getByRole`, `getByLabelText`, `getByPlaceholderText`, `getByText`, `getByDisplayValue`.
2. Semantic queries: `getByAltText`, `getByTitle`.
3. Test IDs: `getByTestId`.

```tsx
// Good: resilient and checks accessibility
screen.getByRole("button", { name: /save changes/i });
screen.getByRole("textbox", { name: "Email" });          // name comes from the <label>
screen.getByRole("heading", { level: 2, name: "Billing" });
screen.getByRole("checkbox", { name: /remember me/i, checked: false });

// Weak: coupled to implementation
container.querySelector(".btn-primary");
screen.getByTestId("save-btn");
```

**Why it matters beyond style:**
- **Free accessibility check**: a clickable `div` without `role="button"` and keyboard support will not be found by `getByRole("button")`. An input without a label will not be found by name. The test fails for the same reason a screen-reader user would be stuck.
- **Refactor resilience**: you can swap a component library, restructure the DOM or rename classes, and the test still passes if the behaviour is the same.
- **Readable tests**: the test reads like a user script.

**Accessible name** is computed from the `label`, `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, or the element's text content. Learning the basic implicit roles helps: `a` with `href` is `link`, `input type="checkbox"` is `checkbox`, `ul` is `list`, `nav` is `navigation`, `dialog` is `dialog`.

**When a test ID is fine**: elements with no meaningful role or text (a chart canvas, a drag handle region), or to disambiguate repeated identical widgets when `within()` scoping is not enough.

**Performance note**: `getByRole` is slower than other queries on very large DOMs because it computes the accessibility tree. For huge lists, scope with `within(region)` first.

**Tooling**: `screen.logTestingPlaygroundURL()` suggests the best query, and `eslint-plugin-testing-library` flags container queries.
followUps: How is an element's accessible name computed?
When is getByTestId acceptable?
Why might getByRole be slow on a very large DOM?
mistakes: Defaulting to test IDs or CSS selectors.
Not connecting role queries to accessibility.
Not knowing that a clickable div is not found as a button.

questions.q: Why is jsdom not a real browser, and when does that matter for your tests?
questions.answer:
**jsdom is a JavaScript implementation of the DOM and some web APIs that runs in Node; it has no rendering engine, so there is no layout, no painting and no real scrolling. That matters whenever behaviour depends on size, position, visibility on screen, real focus and pointer behaviour, or browser APIs jsdom does not implement; for those I use Vitest browser mode, Playwright component tests or E2E tests.**

**What jsdom gives you**: a DOM tree, events, forms, `localStorage`, enough HTML semantics for role queries. That covers most logic-and-state component tests, quickly.

**What it does not do:**
- **Layout**: `getBoundingClientRect()`, `offsetWidth` and `clientHeight` return zeros. Virtualised lists, tooltips that position themselves, "is this truncated?" logic and responsive components behave wrongly.
- **CSS**: limited support; media queries do not respond to a viewport, and `window.matchMedia` is missing unless you stub it.
- **Visibility**: jest-dom's `toBeVisible` checks things like `display: none`, `visibility: hidden` and the `hidden` attribute, but not whether an element is off-screen or covered by another element.
- **Missing APIs**: `IntersectionObserver`, `ResizeObserver`, `scrollIntoView` and others need stubs; canvas needs a separate package.
- **Fidelity**: event details and focus rules are approximations of real browsers.

**The risk**: tests stubbing `IntersectionObserver` to "always intersecting" pass while the real infinite scroll never loads page 2.

**Options when it matters:**

| Need | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| Component behaviour depending on layout or real events | Vitest browser mode (runs tests in a real browser through Playwright or WebdriverIO) |
| Component in isolation in real browsers | Playwright component testing (experimental) or Storybook interaction tests |
| Full flow | Playwright E2E |

```ts
// vitest.config.ts: a separate project for browser tests (sketch)
test: {
  browser: { enabled: true, provider: "playwright", instances: [{ browser: "chromium" }] },
}
```

Exact provider configuration differs between Vitest versions, so follow the current browser mode guide.

**happy-dom** is an alternative to jsdom: often faster, but less complete. You can switch per file with an environment comment.

**My rule**: logic and state in jsdom (fast, most tests), layout and real-browser behaviour in a real browser (fewer, slower tests).
followUps: How would you test an infinite-scroll list that uses IntersectionObserver?
What does toBeVisible actually check?
mistakes: Assuming layout APIs like getBoundingClientRect return real values in jsdom.
Stubbing browser APIs so generously that the test no longer reflects real behaviour.

questions.q: What is the difference between a mock, a stub, a spy and a fake?
questions.answer:
**They are all test doubles, stand-ins for a real dependency. A stub returns canned answers, a spy records how it was called, a mock is set up with expectations about calls and the test verifies those interactions, and a fake is a working but simplified implementation, like an in-memory database. The practical distinction is whether you verify state (the outcome) or behaviour (that a call happened).**

The vocabulary comes from Gerard Meszaros' "xUnit Test Patterns"; Martin Fowler's "Mocks Aren't Stubs" and his "TestDouble" bliki entry are the standard explanations.

| Double | Purpose | Example in a frontend test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dummy | fills a parameter, never used | `onClose={() => {}}` in a test that never closes |
| Stub | returns fixed data | `getUser = () => ({ id: 1, name: "Ada" })` |
| Spy | records calls, may call through | `vi.spyOn(console, "error")` to assert no errors logged |
| Mock | programmed expectations, verified | `expect(track).toHaveBeenCalledWith("checkout_started", { items: 2 })` |
| Fake | simplified real behaviour | MSW handlers backed by an in-memory array; a fake clock |

```ts
// Stub + state verification: assert on the outcome
const getRate = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(0.18);
expect(await priceWithTax(100, getRate)).toBe(118);

// Mock + behaviour verification: the call IS the outcome
const track = vi.fn();
await checkout(cart, { track });
expect(track).toHaveBeenCalledWith("checkout_started", { items: 2 });
```

In Vitest and Jest, `vi.fn()` is technically a spy that you can also give stub behaviour, so the tools blur the terms. What matters is how you use it.

**When to prefer which:**
- **State verification by default**: assert what the user sees or what the function returns. It survives refactors.
- **Behaviour verification when the interaction is the requirement**: an analytics event, a callback prop (`onSubmit` received the right values), a message sent to a parent window.
- **Fakes for complex collaborators**: a stateful in-memory API is more realistic than chains of `mockResolvedValueOnce`, and lets tests do create-then-list flows.

**Pitfall**: heavy behaviour verification on internal collaborators ("the hook called `formatDate` twice") couples tests to implementation, which is the core argument in Fowler's essay between "classicist" and "mockist" styles.
followUps: When is behaviour verification the right choice?
Is vi.fn a mock or a spy?
Why might a fake be better than a chain of mockResolvedValueOnce calls?
mistakes: Using 'mock' for everything without distinguishing state from behaviour verification.
Asserting on calls to internal collaborators instead of outcomes.

questions.q: How do you know when you are over-mocking, and what problems does it cause?
questions.answer:
**You are over-mocking when tests mostly verify your assumptions about collaborators instead of your product: mocks of your own modules and child components, refactors that break many tests without changing behaviour, and production bugs that slip through green tests because the mocks returned shapes the real system never does. The cost is a suite that is both brittle and falsely reassuring.**

**Symptoms:**
- `vi.mock("./OrderRow")` and assertions that the mock received props. That tests JSX wiring.
- Setup longer than the test; nobody can explain why five modules are mocked.
- Behaviour-free assertions: "`useOrders` was called", "`formatPrice` was called twice".
- Renaming a function or splitting a module breaks dozens of tests.
- An incident caused by an API change that every test "covered".

**Why it happens**: mocks make tests easy to write, give high coverage and fast runs, and some codebases inherit a "unit test every file in isolation" rule.

**What it costs:**

| Problem | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| False negatives | safe refactors break tests, so people stop refactoring |
| False positives | tests pass while integration is broken |
| Drift | mocks encode an old contract; reality moved on |
| Review burden | large mock setups hide what is being tested |

**How I fix it:**
1. **Mock only at boundaries**: the network (MSW), time, randomness and vendor SDKs behind a thin adapter. Everything inside the app runs for real.
2. **Integration-first component tests**: render the feature with real children and providers.
3. **Keep mocks honest**: type MSW handlers and fixtures from the OpenAPI schema; add consumer-driven contract tests (for example Pact) for critical APIs; run a few E2E tests against the real backend.
4. **Prefer fakes to mock chains**: an in-memory store behind handlers supports realistic flows.
5. **Delete mock-heavy tests** that duplicate an integration test.

**When heavy mocking is justified**: a failure mode that is hard to produce for real (a timeout halfway through a stream), or a very expensive dependency. Even then, mock at the edge, not inside your own code.

**What the interviewer is testing**: whether you understand that a mock is a claim about the world, and that each claim needs to be checked somewhere, by types, contracts or a real integration run.
followUps: Would you mock child components in a component test?
How do contract tests help?
When is heavy mocking justified?
mistakes: Listing only brittleness and missing false confidence from drifted mocks.
Offering no concrete way to keep mocks honest, such as typed fixtures or contract tests.

questions.q: How does Playwright's auto-waiting work, and why does it reduce flakiness compared to manual sleeps?
questions.answer:
**Before every action Playwright resolves the locator and waits until the element is actionable, for a click that means attached, visible, stable (not animating), enabled and actually receiving pointer events, and its web-first assertions retry until the expected state is reached or a timeout expires. A manual sleep waits a fixed time that is either too short on a slow CI machine or wasted on a fast one, so auto-waiting is both faster and more reliable.**

**What happens on `await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Pay" }).click()`:**

```text
resolve locator (fresh, every attempt)
   -> exactly one match? (strict mode: more than one throws)
   -> attached to DOM?
   -> visible?
   -> stable (same bounding box across animation frames)?
   -> enabled?
   -> receives events (not covered by an overlay or spinner)?
   -> scroll into view, click
   (retry the checks until the action timeout)
```

For `fill`, Playwright also checks the element is editable.

**Web-first assertions** retry the same way:

```ts
await expect(page.getByRole("status")).toHaveText("Payment received"); // retries up to 5 s by default
await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/orders\/\d+/);
await expect(page.getByRole("row")).toHaveCount(3);
```

**Why sleeps cause flakiness:**

```ts
await page.click("#pay");
await page.waitForTimeout(2000);           // anti-pattern
expect(await page.textContent(".status")).toBe("Payment received");
```

- On a loaded CI runner the payment takes 2.3 s and the test fails.
- On a fast laptop it wastes 1.9 s per step, across hundreds of steps.
- It still does not wait for the right thing: a spinner overlay may cover the button.

**Common ways to defeat auto-waiting:**
- One-shot checks: `expect(await locator.isVisible()).toBe(true)` checks once. Use `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()`.
- Reading text with `textContent()` then asserting, instead of `toHaveText`.
- `{ force: true }` on clicks, which skips actionability checks and hides real overlay bugs.

**What auto-waiting does not solve**: test data shared between parallel tests, time-dependent content, and real race conditions in the app. Those still need isolation and deterministic setup. Waiting for a specific network response (`page.waitForResponse`) is occasionally useful, but asserting on the visible result is usually better.
followUps: What does force: true skip, and why is it risky?
What does strict mode do for locators?
Which flakes does auto-waiting not fix?
mistakes: Not naming the actionability checks (visible, stable, enabled, receives events).
Using one-shot checks like isVisible inside expect.
Claiming auto-waiting removes all flakiness.

questions.q: How would you design an end-to-end test suite that stays fast and reliable as the product grows?
questions.answer:
**I keep the E2E suite small and focused on critical journeys, run it against a production build with a seeded, disposable database, make every test independent (own data, isolated browser context, reusable auth state), use only role-based locators and web-first assertions, and scale with parallel workers and sharding. Flakiness is treated as a bug with an owner, and I track suite duration and flake rate as first-class metrics.**

**Scope: what belongs in E2E**
- The journeys that make money or would be catastrophic: sign-up, login, the core create and edit flow, checkout, permissions boundaries.
- Integration between systems that lower layers cannot see: cookies, redirects, real API contracts, migrations.
- Not permutations: validation rules, every error message and UI states go to component tests.

**Architecture of the suite:**

```text
playwright.config.ts
  projects: setup (auth) -> chromium (all tests), webkit + firefox (smoke tag)
  webServer: production build
fixtures/
  data.ts      per-test entities via test API, unique names, teardown
  accounts.ts  worker-scoped accounts with storageState
pages/         small page objects or helper functions for repeated flows
tests/
  checkout.spec.ts  billing.spec.ts  ...
```

**Reliability rules:**
- **Isolation**: each test gets a fresh browser context; it creates its own data via API and never depends on another test's data or order.
- **Locators**: `getByRole`, `getByLabel`; no CSS chains; strict mode catches ambiguity.
- **No sleeps**: auto-waiting actions and web-first assertions only.
- **Deterministic environment**: seeded DB per run, frozen clock where dates matter, third-party services faked at the boundary or sandboxed.
- **Evidence on failure**: traces on first retry, screenshots and videos for failed tests.

**Speed as it grows:**
- `fullyParallel: true`, shard across CI machines and merge blob reports.
- Run Chromium for everything per PR; other browsers on a smoke tag per PR or nightly.
- API-based setup instead of clicking through prerequisites.
- Optional: run tests affected by changed areas on PRs and the full suite on `main`.

**Governance:**
- A rule for adding E2E tests: "could a component test catch this?" If yes, write that instead.
- Flake tracking per test; quarantine with owner and deadline.
- Budget: for example, "the E2E lane must give a result in under 10 minutes"; when it grows past that, shard more or prune.

**Trade-off**: per-test data creation and per-worker accounts add fixture complexity, but shared fixtures are the main reason large E2E suites become flaky.
followUps: How do you decide whether a new test belongs in E2E?
How do you handle third-party services like payments?
What metrics would you track for the suite?
mistakes: Covering permutations and edge cases in E2E instead of component tests.
Shared test data and order-dependent tests.
No plan for flakiness or suite duration.

questions.q: How do you test a Next.js app that uses React Server Components?
questions.answer:
**I split it by what the code is: pure logic and data functions get unit tests, synchronous Server Components and all Client Components can be tested with Vitest and React Testing Library, and async Server Components, routing, Server Actions and caching behaviour are covered by Playwright E2E tests against a production build, which is what the Next.js testing docs recommend for async Server Components today.**

**Why RSC complicates testing**: an async Server Component runs only on the server, awaits data inside the component, and is streamed to the client. React Testing Library renders on the client and cannot render async components the way the Next.js server does. The Next.js Vitest guide notes that Vitest does not currently support async Server Components and recommends E2E tests for them.

**A layered approach:**

```text
lib/ (data access, business rules)        -> Vitest unit tests
server actions (validation + mutation)    -> unit test the pure parts (zod schema,
                                             permission checks); E2E for the full flow
client components                         -> Vitest + RTL + MSW
sync server components                    -> RTL can render them like normal components
async server components, routes, caching  -> Playwright on next build && next start
```

**Make server code testable by design:**

```ts
// app/orders/page.tsx stays thin
export default async function OrdersPage() {
  const session = await requireSession();
  const orders = await listOrders(session.userId); // tested separately
  return <OrdersTable orders={orders} />;          // presentational, testable with RTL
}
```

Keep the async component a thin shell that fetches and passes data to presentational components, and move rules into plain functions. Most of the logic is then covered by fast tests; the E2E test only verifies wiring.

**E2E specifics:**
- Test a production build (`next build` then `next start`), not `next dev`: caching, prerendering and streaming behave differently.
- Seed the database and reset it per run.
- Verify Server Actions end to end: submit the form, assert the updated UI, reload and assert persistence.
- For caching and revalidation, assert behaviour: update data through the API, trigger the revalidation path, check the page shows the new value.

**Trade-off**: more of the suite sits at the slow E2E layer than in a pure client app, which is why keeping server components thin matters.
followUps: Why test against next build and next start rather than next dev?
How would you test a Server Action?
How do you keep async server components thin?
mistakes: Assuming RTL can render async Server Components like client components.
Putting business logic inside async components where only E2E tests can reach it.

questions.q: What is visual regression testing, and what makes screenshot tests flaky?
questions.answer:
**Visual regression testing renders a page or component, screenshots it, and compares it pixel by pixel against an approved baseline, failing when the difference exceeds a threshold. Screenshot tests are flaky because pixels depend on everything: OS and font rendering, fonts loading late, animations, dates and random data, dynamic content, lazy images and viewport size. The fix is to remove those sources of noise, not to raise the tolerance.**

**What it catches that functional tests miss**: a button that became invisible due to a colour token change, a layout pushed out of place by a padding change, broken styles after a CSS library upgrade, dark-mode regressions.

**The workflow:**

```text
render -> screenshot -> compare with baseline -> pass
                                  |
                              diff > threshold -> fail with diff image
                                  |
                        human: bug (fix code) or intended (update baseline)
```

In Playwright: `await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot("pricing.png", { maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01 })`. The first run writes the baseline; `--update-snapshots` regenerates after intended changes. Baselines are named per browser and platform because rendering differs.

**Sources of flakiness and their fixes:**

| Noise | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| OS, GPU, font rasterisation | run in one pinned Docker image locally and in CI |
| Web fonts loading after the screenshot | self-host fonts, wait for `document.fonts.ready` |
| Animations, transitions, caret | disabled by default in `toHaveScreenshot`; respect reduced motion |
| Timestamps, "2 minutes ago" | freeze the clock |
| Random or live data | seeded fixtures, MSW, or `mask` the region |
| Lazy images, skeletons | wait for the final content to be present |
| Scrollbars, viewport differences | fixed viewport per project, hide scrollbars |
| Sub-pixel anti-aliasing | a small tolerance (`threshold`, `maxDiffPixelRatio`) |

**Why a big tolerance is wrong**: if 5% of pixels may change, a missing icon or a wrong price passes. Keep tolerances tight and stabilise the input.

**Human factor**: if diffs are noisy, reviewers accept everything and the suite is worthless. Small, well-named snapshots and a clear approval step make the diffs reviewable.
followUps: How do you handle a component that shows the current date?
Why are baselines platform-specific?
What tolerance would you choose?
mistakes: Raising the diff tolerance to hide flakes.
Generating baselines on a laptop and comparing on Linux CI.
Not mentioning fonts, animations and dynamic data.

questions.q: How would you set up visual regression testing for a component library?
questions.answer:
**I would use Storybook as the catalogue of every component state, snapshot each story in each theme and key viewport, and run the comparison either with a hosted service like Chromatic (per-branch baselines, review UI, TurboSnap to snapshot only affected stories) or self-hosted with Playwright's `toHaveScreenshot` in a pinned Docker image. The real work is determinism and a review workflow designers and engineers actually use.**

**1. Stories as test cases.** Every meaningful state gets a story: default, hover and focus, disabled, loading, error, long text, empty, right-to-left, light and dark themes. Stories double as documentation and as interaction and accessibility test targets.

**2. Choose the runner:**

| Option | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chromatic | cloud browsers, branch baselines, review UI, TurboSnap | paid beyond free tier, external service |
| Playwright self-hosted | free, full control, baselines in repo | you own determinism, storage and review |
| Other hosted (Percy, Applitools) | similar review workflows; Applitools adds visual AI comparison | cost, vendor lock-in |

A self-hosted sketch: read Storybook's generated `index.json`, visit each story's iframe URL, and screenshot it:

```ts
for (const story of stories) {
  test(`${story.title} ${story.name}`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto(`/iframe.html?id=${story.id}&globals=theme:dark`);
    await page.evaluate(() => document.fonts.ready);
    await expect(page.locator("#storybook-root")).toHaveScreenshot(`${story.id}-dark.png`);
  });
}
```

**3. Determinism:**
- Pinned Docker image matching the Playwright version, used locally and in CI.
- Self-hosted fonts, frozen dates via a global decorator, seeded data, MSW for any network.
- Animations off; tight tolerances.

**4. Scope and cost:** components x states x themes x viewports grows fast. Snapshot components in both themes at one viewport, responsive components at two, and a few composed pages. Use changed-file detection (TurboSnap or your own) on PRs; full runs on `main`.

**5. Workflow:**
- Required PR check; the author reviews diffs, design reviews intentional visual changes.
- Baselines updated in the same PR as the change.
- Release notes generated for consumers when visual changes are approved.

**6. Pair with other checks**: axe on every story, interaction tests for behaviour, and type checks on the component API. Visual tests tell you something changed; they do not tell you it is correct.
followUps: Would you use a hosted service or self-host?
How do you keep the number of snapshots manageable?
Who approves visual diffs?
mistakes: Snapshotting full pages only, giving noisy diffs.
No plan for determinism or review workflow.
Ignoring cost as stories x themes x viewports multiply.

questions.q: How do you prevent performance regressions from reaching production?
questions.answer:
**I put automated guards at three points: in the PR, byte budgets on bundles and Lighthouse CI assertions on key pages against a production build; at release, real-user monitoring of Core Web Vitals per route with alerts on regressions after deploys; and for the backend, load tests with percentile thresholds on the APIs critical pages depend on. Each guard has an owner and a defined response when it fails.**

**1. In the pull request**

- **Bundle budgets** (deterministic, so not flaky): `size-limit` or similar per entry point, with the delta posted on the PR ("+42 kB gzipped: imported the full icon set").
- **Lighthouse CI** on 3 to 5 representative URLs, multiple runs per URL, asserting on specific metrics:

```js
assertions: {
  "largest-contentful-paint": ["error", { maxNumericValue: 2500 }],
  "cumulative-layout-shift": ["error", { maxNumericValue: 0.1 }],
  "total-blocking-time": ["warn", { maxNumericValue: 200 }],
  "resource-summary:script:size": ["error", { maxNumericValue: 300000 }],
}
```

- **Static checks**: lint rules against importing heavy libraries in client components, image components that require dimensions (prevents CLS).

**2. In production**

- `web-vitals` library reporting LCP, INP and CLS with route and device class to analytics or a RUM tool.
- Dashboards at p75 per route; alerts when a metric crosses the "good" threshold (LCP 2.5 s, INP 200 ms, CLS 0.1) or worsens noticeably after a deploy.
- Annotate deploys on the dashboards so regressions map to a release; feature flags or rollback to respond quickly.

**3. Backend dependencies**

- k6 tests on critical endpoints with thresholds such as `p(95)<300` and error rate below 1%; a smoke run on PRs and a full load test nightly or before launches.

**4. Process**

- A performance budget agreed with product: what we commit to, per page type.
- When a budget fails: optimise, or raise it consciously with a written reason. No silent bumps.
- Third-party scripts go through the same budget; they are a common source of regressions.

**Pitfalls**: failing builds on noisy single Lighthouse runs (the team disables the check), measuring the dev server, and lab-only monitoring that misses what real devices experience.
followUps: How do you stop Lighthouse checks from being flaky?
What happens when a budget fails?
How do you budget third-party scripts?
mistakes: Relying on a single Lighthouse score from one run.
Having lab checks only, with no field monitoring.
Budgets without an owner or a response process.

questions.q: Lab data says the page is fast but field data says it is slow. How do you explain and resolve that?
questions.answer:
**Lab data is one synthetic load on one device and network profile; field data is the 75th percentile of many real visits on real devices, networks, cache states and interactions. The gap usually comes from slower real devices, different LCP elements per viewport, personalised or logged-in pages, third-party scripts, cold caches and interactions during load. I resolve it by segmenting the field data to find who is slow and where, reproducing that condition in the lab, fixing it, and confirming with field data after release.**

**Why they differ** (web.dev's "Why lab and field data can be different" covers these):
- **Devices**: a CI machine, even throttled, is not a budget Android phone with thermal throttling.
- **Network**: real users have high-latency, variable connections; some are far from your CDN region.
- **Cache state**: lab runs are often cold or always warm; real visits mix both, and returning users may have service workers.
- **Content**: logged-in or personalised pages, A/B variants, cookie banners and ads that the lab run never sees.
- **Viewport**: the LCP element on mobile may be a hero image, on desktop a heading.
- **Interaction**: INP only exists in the field; users click while the main thread is busy hydrating.
- **Distribution**: lab is one sample; field is p75, so a slow tail of users dominates.

**Resolving it step by step:**

```text
1. segment field data: route, device class, country, connection, logged-in vs not
2. find the dominant slow segment and metric (e.g. INP on mid-range Android, product page)
3. use attribution: web-vitals attribution build gives the LCP element, the slow interaction target,
   and the long animation frames or scripts behind it
4. reproduce in the lab with matching conditions: CPU throttling, mobile viewport,
   logged-in state, the real third-party tags
5. fix, ship behind a flag if risky, watch p75 for that segment over the following days
```

**Typical findings:**
- INP poor because a large hydration or an analytics script blocks clicks during load; the lab only showed high TBT, which nobody had asserted on.
- LCP poor on mobile because the hero image is lazy-loaded or not prioritised.
- CLS from a consent banner or late-loading ad slot that only appears for real users.

**Important nuance**: CrUX and similar field datasets aggregate over 28 days, so improvements show up gradually. Your own RUM gives faster feedback.

**What not to do**: declare victory because Lighthouse shows 95. The field data is what users experience and what Google Search uses.
followUps: Why can't Lighthouse measure INP?
How would you find which interaction is slow?
How long until a fix shows in CrUX?
mistakes: Trusting the lab score over field data.
Not segmenting field data by device, route and user state.
Not knowing INP is field-only.

questions.q: A test fails 1 in 20 runs on CI but never locally. How do you investigate it?
questions.answer:
**I treat it as a real race until proven otherwise: reproduce it by running the test many times under CI-like conditions, collect evidence from CI (trace, screenshots, logs), check whether it depends on other tests, timing, the clock or the environment, and fix the root cause rather than adding a sleep or a retry. "Never locally" usually means a difference in speed, parallelism, data or environment between my machine and CI.**

**1. Reproduce**
- Repeat it: `npx playwright test checkout.spec.ts --repeat-each=50 --workers=4`, or loop Vitest on the file.
- Match CI: same Docker image, same worker count, CPU throttling or a smaller machine, `CI=true`, the same `TZ` and locale.
- Run the full file or suite with shuffled order (`--sequence.shuffle` in Vitest) to expose order dependence.

**2. Read the evidence**
- Playwright trace from the failed attempt: DOM snapshot at the failing step, network calls (a 500? a slow response?), console errors.
- Test history: does it fail on a particular shard, time of day, or since a specific commit?

**3. Classify the cause**

| Clue | Likely cause |
| --- | --- |
| Fails only with other tests | shared data, leaked mocks, global state |
| Fails on slow runners | missing await, one-shot assertion, too-tight timeout, sleep |
| Fails near midnight UTC or month end | date logic or timezone |
| Fails on one shard | data collision with another test in that shard |
| Element "not stable" or "intercepts pointer events" | animation or overlay still present |
| Different data each run | randomness or a shared environment |

**4. Fix the cause**
- Replace sleeps and one-shot checks with web-first assertions or `findBy`.
- Give the test its own data with unique names; reset MSW handlers and mocks.
- Freeze time; seed randomness.
- If the trace shows a real app race (double submit, stale response overwrites newer data), fix the app; that bug also hits users.

**5. Prove it**: rerun 50 to 100 times on CI-like settings with zero failures, then merge.

**While investigating**: if it blocks the team, quarantine it with a ticket and an owner rather than letting everyone rerun pipelines. Do not "fix" with retries or a longer timeout without understanding why; that just moves the flake.
followUps: How do you tell a test bug from an app race condition?
What artefacts would you configure CI to keep?
How do you prove the fix worked?
mistakes: Adding a sleep, a longer timeout or a retry without finding the cause.
Not trying to reproduce under CI-like conditions with repeated runs.
Dismissing the possibility of a real app bug.

questions.q: What is your policy for flaky tests: retry, quarantine or delete?
questions.answer:
**All three, in that order and with limits: retries on CI only, reported as flaky rather than passed so they are measured; automatic detection and quarantine for tests that keep flaking, with a ticket, an owner and a deadline; and deletion if the test is not fixed by the deadline or adds little value. The goal is that a red build always means a real problem, so the team never learns to rerun until green.**

**Why a policy at all**: Google's testing blog reported about 1.5% of test runs being flaky and almost 16% of tests showing some flakiness. At scale, flakes are constant, and without a policy, trust in CI erodes and real failures get rerun into production.

**Retries**
- Playwright `retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0`. A test that fails then passes is marked flaky in the report.
- Never on locally, so developers notice flakes while writing tests.
- Retries are a buffer, not a fix; the flaky result is data.

**Detection**
- Store results from every CI run (JUnit or Playwright JSON). A test is flagged when it passes only after retry, or has mixed results on the same commit.
- Compute a flake rate per test over a window, for example the last 50 runs on `main`. Slack Engineering's "Handling Flaky Tests at Scale" describes automating detection and suppression like this.
- Separate infrastructure failures (runner died, install failed) before scoring.

**Quarantine**

```ts
test("bulk export completes", { tag: "@quarantine" }, async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });
```

- Blocking job runs `--grep-invert @quarantine`; a non-blocking job runs quarantined tests and records results.
- Every quarantine opens a ticket assigned to the owning team, with the trace attached.
- Quarantine size is a visible metric; a growing list is a health warning.

**Fix or delete**
- Deadline, for example 2 weeks. Fixing means finding the root cause (often async timing, shared data or a real app race).
- If unfixed or low value, delete it and, if the behaviour matters, write a better test at a cheaper layer.

**What I avoid**
- Infinite retries or retrying whole pipelines.
- Quarantine without an owner, which is silent deletion with extra steps.
- Blaming the tool: Playwright's auto-waiting removes many timing flakes, but not data and isolation problems.

**Trade-off**: quarantine temporarily reduces coverage of that behaviour. For critical journeys, fix immediately rather than quarantine.
followUps: How would you detect flaky tests automatically?
Would you quarantine a test for the checkout journey?
What would you do if the quarantine list keeps growing?
mistakes: Choosing only one option, such as unlimited retries.
Quarantine without an owner or deadline.
Enabling retries locally so developers never see flakes.

questions.q: How would you cut a 40-minute frontend CI pipeline down to under 10 minutes?
questions.answer:
**First I measure where the 40 minutes go, then attack the biggest items: run independent checks in parallel instead of in sequence, cache dependencies, browsers and build outputs, build once and reuse the artefact, shard the E2E suite across machines, run only affected tasks on PRs in a monorepo, and move or delete slow low-value tests. Most pipelines that slow are serial and uncached rather than doing too much work.**

**1. Measure**: timing per job and step over the last N runs, and the slowest tests from the reporters. Typical breakdown of a slow pipeline:

```text
install 4m -> lint 3m -> typecheck 4m -> unit 8m -> build 6m -> e2e 15m   (serial: 40m)
```

**2. Parallelise the fast lane**

```text
install (cached, ~40s)
  |-- lint        |-- typecheck     |-- unit (sharded)     |-- build
                                                               |
                                              e2e shard 1..4 (on the build artefact)
```

Critical path becomes roughly install + build + slowest E2E shard.

**3. Cache**
- `actions/setup-node` with `cache: npm` (or pnpm), keyed on the lockfile.
- Playwright browsers cached by version, or use the official Playwright Docker image.
- Build and task caching with Turborepo or Nx (remote cache), so unchanged packages are not rebuilt or retested.
- Incremental TypeScript (`tsc --build` with project references) and ESLint cache.

**4. Build once**: upload the production build as an artefact; E2E, Lighthouse and visual jobs download it instead of rebuilding.

**5. Shard**: `npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/4` with `fullyParallel: true` for even shards, blob reports merged at the end. Vitest also supports `--shard`.

**6. Do less work per PR**
- Affected-only tasks in a monorepo; the full suite on `main` and before release.
- Chromium only on PRs; Firefox and WebKit nightly or on a smoke tag.
- Move permutation-heavy E2E tests down to component tests.
- Faster environments where safe: happy-dom for simple component tests, avoid unnecessary isolation overhead.

**7. Fix the slow tests**: sleeps, UI-based setup instead of API setup, logging in per test instead of reusing `storageState`, huge fixtures.

**8. Keep it fast**: track pipeline p50 and p95 duration as a metric, budget it ("mergeable signal in under 10 minutes"), and review when it drifts.

**Trade-offs**: more shards cost more CI minutes and have setup overhead per machine; affected-only runs can miss indirect breakage, so the full suite must still run on `main` or in a merge queue.
followUps: Why doesn't doubling shards halve the time?
What are the risks of running only affected tests?
What would you cache and how would you key it?
mistakes: Jumping to more machines before measuring where time goes.
Rebuilding the app in every job instead of building once.
Forgetting that the full suite still needs to run on main.
